سَيَاعٌ , (K,) or سِيَاعٌ, (S,) or both, (MF, TA,) Mud: (TA:) or mud [mixed] with chopped straw, with which one plasters. (Kr, S, K.) The saying of the poet, (S, K,) namely El-Kutámee, (K,) describing his she-camel, (TA,) “فَلَمَّا أَنْ جَرَى سِمَنٌ عَلَيْهَا
كَمَا طَيَّنْتَ بِالفَدَنِ السَّيَاعَا
” presents an inversion, the meaning being كما طيّنت بِالسِيَّاعِ الفَدَنِ [i. e. And when fatness extended upon her, as when thou plasterest with mud and chopped straw the pavilion]; الفَدَن signifying القَصْر. (S, K: [but in the former, only the latter hemistich is cited; and in some copies of the former, and in the O, we find بَطَّنْتَ in the place of طَيَّنْتَ.]) ―
-b2- Also Fat with which a مَزَادَة [or leathern water-bag] is anointed. (K.) ―
-b3- And (tropical:) Pitch, or tar; syn. زِفْتٌ; as being likened to mud, because of its blackness. (TA.)
From An Arabic-English Lexicon (Edward William Lane)
